1:
The verse begins with no date attached to it, and the commentators fill the gap differently. Ellicott points out that the opening word is simply and in the original, with no note of time at all, and takes the many days to run until near the close of the thirty-ninth year; the direction, by the way of the Red sea, he reads as southward, toward the gulf of Akabah. Wesley glosses Mount Seir as the mountainous country of Edom and puts the period at thirty-eight years. Gill notices what the turn meant in practice — from Kadesh, on whose borders they had stood, they now set their backs to the land of Canaan. Calvin values the verse precisely for the join it makes: Numbers does not say when they struck camp, so without this notice what follows would come abruptly; and he reads the manner of the journey as its own lesson, since by wearying themselves to no purpose in circuitous wandering they might at length learn to follow God directly and not decline from the way he points out.

Henry makes the delay purposeful on two sides at once. For Israel it was chastisement for murmuring and unbelief, but also preparation — humbling them for sin, teaching them to mortify their lusts, to follow God and to comfort themselves in him; it is a work of time, he says, to make souls meet for heaven, and it must be done by a long train of exercises. For the Canaanites it was preparation of another kind. All those years the measure of their iniquity was filling up, and a space that might have been improved for repentance was abused to the hardening of their hearts; having seen the host of Israel once repulsed and then so long entangled and seemingly lost in the wilderness, they grew secure and reckoned the danger from that quarter past, which would only make the next attempt the more dreadful. Henry's summary of the whole is that though God contend long he will not contend for ever, and that a people kept waiting for deliverance will have it at last, the vision being for an appointed time.

The turn northward is described by the map rather than the calendar. Keil and Delitzsch have them go through the Arabah to its southern extremity and then round the southern end of Mount Seir, proceeding north along its eastern side without making war on the Edomites; Clarke makes the same point by contrast, that this was not the road they had taken before by Kadesh-barnea, but a route between Edom on one hand and Moab and Ammon on the other, bringing them into Canaan through the land of the Amorites. Wesley says the same in a phrase.

Ellicott turns the itinerary into a question nobody can settle. He places the command at Kadesh the second time, early in the fortieth year, and then asks when it was decided that Israel should enter by crossing Jordan rather than going up through the south country. If Edom had gained territory westward during the thirty-eight years, permission would have been needed to go by the way of the spies, and the decision to cross Jordan might have followed Edom's refusal; but if, as Conder supposes, what was asked was leave to pass eastward between the mountains, then the decision must have been taken earlier — for the same reason given at the exodus, that the people should not have to fight their way in. On that reading, he observes, the miraculous entry across Jordan becomes still more closely analogous to the miraculous departure from Egypt.
4:
The charge is given before the request it anticipates. Ellicott reads the clause literally as ye are passing through the border, and takes it to have been spoken in view of the permission Moses was about to ask — permission Edom then refused; the fear he refers to the song of Moses, where the dukes of Edom were foretold to be amazed. Gill and Clarke put the prohibition plainly: they were neither to contend with the Edomites in battle nor to provoke them to it.

Calvin measures how hard that was to bear. The trial lay not only in hearing beforehand that the embassy would be fruitless, but in being told that even if Edom met them with injustice and hostility they must still keep their hands from arms. There would have been some reason in the first part — a request presented in a friendly way and rejected gives a lawful cause of war — but the further condition, that they might do nothing whatever against men who refused them quiet passage, could well seem intolerable, since it left them worse off than the common law of nations allowed. That they took it at all is the point: it shows how far thirty-eight years of wandering and various chastisement had gone toward subduing a people who would otherwise have exclaimed loudly that God had dealt unkindly with them.

Ellicott finds something worth remarking in the reason God gives for the prohibition. Esau's inheritance was won before Jacob's, as Ishmael's line developed before Isaac's: while Isaac and Israel were still strangers and sojourners, the Ishmaelites were already princes with towns and castles and the Edomites had their dukes and their kings.

On buying rather than taking, the commentators are careful about what the permission implies. Gill reports Aben Ezra's reading that they might buy if they chose — the manna still fell daily, but other food could be had when opportunity offered, provided it was paid for and not seized or stolen — and notes an alternative construction of the clause as a question, shall ye buy meat?, answered by the sufficiency God had already given. Wesley allows the purchase and forbids only the appetite, that they should not greedily hunger after such food when they could not get it; and he explains the buying of water by the scarcity of it in those parts, where private persons dug their own pits. Ellicott sets the whole arrangement beside Abram refusing to enrich himself from the king of Sodom.

Why they should buy when they could have plundered is answered from their own prosperity. Clarke has it that God had given them much property, so that they had no need of spoil and had gold and silver to pay with, and would therefore not permit them to take anything by violence; Wesley draws the same conclusion more sharply, that theft would have been inexcusable in men who could not plead necessity. Calvin raises the obvious objection — how could God be said to have blessed the work of their hands when they had no commerce with anyone to profit by? His answer is that although they were sustained gratuitously and had not spent a penny on so much as a shoelatchet, their cattle had increased and their daily labour had yielded something, not in wages but in the furniture and necessaries they made for themselves. Ellicott answers it the other way, seeing nothing unreasonable in supposing they acquired wealth by trade or ordinary occupations along the road, since there were skilled workmen among them.
8:
Henry stops on a word before anything else. Speaking of Edom, Moses calls them our brethren, the children of Esau, though they had lately refused Israel a peaceable passage; and Henry takes the choice deliberately — when our relations fail in their duty to us, we must keep a sense of the relation and not fail in ours to them as occasion offers. Keil and Delitzsch find the same principle in the text itself: the Edomites are called Israel's brethren and the Moabites the sons of Lot for the same reason, that the bond of blood-relationship with these tribes was to be held sacred. Calvin adds that the ground of the favour was not what the nations had deserved, since God did not take their deserts into account at all, but that they were descended from Lot and so of the stock of Abraham.

The route is given by its landmarks. Keil and Delitzsch have Israel go past the Edomite mountains by way of the Arabah, from Elath and Ezion-geber, into the steppes of Moab where they were encamped as Moses spoke; Gill puts it more simply, that they went along the borders of their kinsmen's country. At the Moabite frontier the same prohibition was repeated, since Ar had been given to the children of Lot. Calvin marks how much harder the second charge was to keep than the first: they were to cherish kindness and fraternal goodwill toward people who treated them with hostility, and God meant by it to prove their obedience. Ellicott notes the pattern the two prohibitions make together — the children of Lot, like those of Ishmael and Esau, had their earthly inheritance before the children of Abraham had theirs.

At this point Moses interrupts himself, and both Calvin and Keil say so explicitly. The ninth verse runs on regularly into the thirteenth, and what stands between is a parenthesis of the writer's own, inserted to confirm that Moab and Edom held their lands by the same divine grant Israel was claiming — Lot, after all, had been as much an alien as Abraham, and Moses is explaining how his posterity came by a territory of their own.

The earlier inhabitants are described and then disputed. Gill traces the Emim back to the campaign of Chedorlaomer, when they dwelt at Kirjathaim, and derives their name from the terror their stature and strength inspired; Wesley reads their expulsion by Moab as encouragement to Israel, since God would much more drive out the accursed Canaanites for his own people. Clarke resists the whole picture. He follows Calmet in supposing them destroyed in that early war, and thinks they were probably a hardy, fierce and terrible people living like wandering Arabs on the plunder of others, which was enough by itself to earn them the name of giants. He objects outright to the translation in the next verse: the word is not giants but Rephaim, the name of a people, and Emim, Anakim and Rephaim were most likely one race called by different names in the different countries they occupied. He grants that there were men of extraordinary stature among them, but adds that fear and public report have often added to what was there.

The Horim are obscurer still. Gill cannot say who they were or where the name came from, but supposes it taken from their living in holes and caves in the rocks of southern Idumea, which would make them the people the Greeks called Troglodytae; Keil and Delitzsch, glossing the name the same way as cave-dwellers, call their origin altogether involved in obscurity. Clarke suspects the verse itself is a later insertion by Joshua or Ezra, where Keil argues the closing comparison with Israel's own possession presupposes nothing of the kind. Wesley disposes of the difficulty grammatically instead, taking the past tense for a future after the manner of the prophets.
13:
Calvin picks up the thread the parenthesis had dropped. God had commanded them to pass by Seir and go forward to Zered, which is as much as to say that a people subdued by their own misfortunes were forbidden any further advance until God opened the way — so that they should follow him as their leader instead of making a passage at their own discretion. Keil and Delitzsch give the same movement geographically: they were to leave the desert bounding Moab on the east, cross the brook, and press on toward the country of the Amorites.

Where the brook was nobody can say. Gill notes that it is called a valley elsewhere and that the word carries both senses, so that very probably there were a valley and a brook of the same name, somewhere near Dibon-gad. Ellicott admits it is still unidentified, and offers two possibilities — one of the several streams running into the Dead Sea south of Arnon, or a tributary of Arnon itself. He is more confident about the name than the place. The root means to prune, and the word denotes the luxuriant growth and young shoots, particularly of the willow, that are cut away with the knife; the Targum takes it so, and the valley was likely named for the willows of its brook. From which he draws a figure and does not apologise for it: this was the valley of pruning in another sense for the vine God had brought out of Egypt, the last of the fruitless branches being taken away here so that the vine might bring forth more fruit.

The thirty-eight years are then counted out. Keil and Delitzsch date the crossing from the condemnation at Kadesh and mark that the rejected generation had by then entirely disappeared — not all of them by a natural death, since the hand of the Lord was against them, a phrase they connect with the terrors by which he destroys his enemies, working through extraordinary judgments. Gill itemises what those were: the sword of Amalek, the plague at Shittim in which twenty-four thousand died, the destruction of Korah and his company and the plague of fourteen thousand seven hundred that followed hard upon it — one stroke after another until the work was done. Calvin explains who was covered by the sentence, men of war meaning those whose age entitled them to bear arms, above twenty; and where forty years are named elsewhere, he says, the two spent at Sinai and on the way are being counted in, and rightly, since during those also their sins were keeping them out of their inheritance.

Ellicott reads the same fact as evidence about the writer. That the last of the older generation is said to have been wasted out precisely at Zered indicates an intimate knowledge of the incidents of the exodus — the census did not take place until some months later, and a plague intervened. He also imagines the human situation behind the notice. As the survivors grew fewer they would become marked men; every one of them who had passed the muster at Sinai was under sentence; and by the time they reached this brook the fortieth year was more than half spent, so that all who were still alive knew they had a short time to live. Probably, he supposes, more notice was taken of the last few deaths than of all the rest of the six hundred thousand together. The best comment on the whole discipline he finds in the ninetieth Psalm, where the secret sins are set in the light of God's countenance and all the days pass away in his wrath.
17:
The word comes after the crossing, and Gill places it at the brook or at the next station. What it directs is a march along the Moabite frontier and then past a second kinsman without touching him. Gill takes the passing over Ar to mean crossing the Arnon by the city that stood on it, and Ellicott records Conder's identification of that city with a ruin north of Merah. Keil and Delitzsch tie the timing to the deaths just recorded: only when the condemned generation had quite died out did the Lord make known that they were to cross Moab's boundary and come opposite the children of Ammon, who lay to the east — and there too they were to leave the descendants of Lot alone, since God would give them nothing of a land already granted.

Calvin finds the grant harder to account for here than in the earlier cases, and does not smooth it over. Ammon and Moab were both born of an incestuous connection, and the memory of their origin was detestable; on the face of it it would have been more reasonable for so tragic a circumstance to be buried in their destruction than for these two nations to be marked out for divine favour above the common lot, as though their descent made them superior. His conclusion is not an explanation but a posture: God's judgments are a deep abyss beyond our apprehension, and are to be regarded with reverence. What he will say positively is that Lot's piety is expressly declared in Scripture, and that God so marked the disgraceful act committed in drunkenness with perpetual infamy as still to leave signs of mercy upon it — chiefly, he thinks, for Abraham's sake. And he reads the whole notice as addressed to Israel's own conduct: they are told whose posterity these are so that they may deal kindly with two nations they can see God himself caring for, on the ground of a relationship they share.

The same argument that established Edom's and Moab's title is then applied to Ammon. Calvin's reasoning is that the Ammonites, in conquering and overthrowing giants, had passed the limits of ordinary human bravery, which is itself proof of unusual favour — since neither could two men have increased by any ordinary course of nature into so great a multitude.

Where those giants came from Calvin cannot settle, and he says so at some length. Taking Caphtor for Cappadocia on the authority of the learned, he observes that we do not actually know whether the people Ammon dispossessed sprang from there. If they did, then a long journey attended by many dangers lies behind them, and something else needs explaining: men who must have passed through rich and fertile country on the way should not have ended in the mountains. His guess is that a band making forays as robbers might find no quiet resting place anywhere until some less cultivated region offered one — which would account for a people settling where the land was poorest. He offers it as a guess and leaves it there, one of the few places in this chapter where a commentator admits he is filling a gap rather than reading a text.
20:
Who these earlier peoples were, nobody can say with confidence. Clarke calls the Ammonite territory the land of the Rephaim, identifies the Zamzummim with the Zuzim of the campaign in Genesis, and admits that very little is known of them — probably inconsiderable tribes or clans, pursuing and pursued, each other's prey, until a stronger power destroyed or subdued them and their name either died out or was swallowed in the conqueror's. Ellicott makes the same identification in a phrase. Gill puts the case from the other side, that the Zamzummim were so numerous and of such stature that Ammon could never have prevailed against them unaided.

Ellicott then draws the argument the whole passage exists to make. By setting the conquest of Canaan beside conquests of gigantic races already achieved by Edom, Moab and Ammon, Moses brings the coming campaign into the domain of ordinary history — and the inference is plain enough: if the children of Lot and Ishmael and Esau, Gentiles for all their descent from Abraham, were able to dispossess such races, how much more should Israel be able to dispossess the Canaanites under the personal guidance of God?

The last of the four displacements lies furthest from Moses' road and is told for the pattern rather than the geography. Gill identifies the Avim with the Avites who seem to have held part of the Philistine country as far as Gaza, and takes the place-name for a common noun: the word signifies courts, which a learned man interprets of tents or huts set in a square or circle with an open area in the middle, and in such the Avim may be supposed to have lived. Ellicott agrees it should be rendered in villages rather than treated as a proper name, since it occurs nowhere else as one, is plural in form, and bears that sense elsewhere; and he glosses the second name as Gaza.

Where the conquerors came from is less settled. Ellicott connects the Caphtorim with the prophet's word that the Philistines came from Caphtor, and reports that some make the country Cyprus or Crete. Wesley makes them a people akin to the Philistines and confederate with them in the enterprise, who by dwelling together and by degrees intermarrying became one people; he takes Caphtor for Cappadocia, and guesses they might have made the expedition out of Egypt either on reports of that country's riches, which drew others from equally remote places, or for some reason now past finding out. What Ellicott notices about the notice itself is where it puts the Philistines: whatever else is uncertain, the verse makes Philistia the scene of a conquest, so that the people Joshua would meet there were themselves a nation holding land taken from someone else.

Clarke stands back from all four notices and observes that these two blocks of verses sit apart from the narrative around them, a single interpolated survey of who held these countries before their present owners. Gill draws the plainest form of the lesson by repetition — God did for Esau what he did for Ammon, and for Moab what he did for both — and the repetition is the argument. Every neighbour Israel was now forbidden to touch was living on ground taken from a taller and older people, and not one of them had taken it unaided.
24:
Henry reads the commission as a reward for what came before. God had tried his people's self-denial by forbidding them to meddle with Moab and Ammon, and they had passed quietly by rich countries they outnumbered; now they are given Sihon's. If we forbear what God forbids, he says, we shall receive what he promises and be no losers by obedience, however much it may look like loss at the time — wrong not others, and God shall right thee. Keil and Delitzsch put the contrast without the moral: the kindred tribes were not to be touched in the possessions God had given them, but the Amorites, who had forced their way into Gilead and Bashan, were given into Israel's hands. Ellicott supplies what makes that defensible: the territory from Arnon northward had been taken from Moab by the Amorites in the first place.

Two things in the wording Henry will not let pass. Though God assures them the land shall be theirs, they must still contend in battle: what God gives, we must endeavour to get. And though they must fight, he fights too — begin to possess it, and I will begin to put the dread of you upon them — so that one act dispirits the enemy and magnifies Israel. Keil and Delitzsch date that promise to the day of the crossing, and Gill hears in it the fulfilment of what Moses had prophesied at the sea; Ellicott sets it beside the song's words that fear and dread should fall on the inhabitants of Canaan. Wesley enters the one qualification the text makes: the nations under the whole heaven are restrained by the clause following to those who heard the report.

Whether the order of events has been kept is Calvin's question, and he answers no. The embassy described a few verses on he takes for a parenthesis, to be read in the pluperfect — I had sent — so that the commission to attack came after the messengers returned empty. On that reading the sequence is consolation as much as order: Sihon has not repudiated the offered peace with impunity, and it is lawful war Israel is now sent into. He supports the arrangement from the later verse about Sihon's hardening, which repeats the movement in different words.

Henry looks past the commission to what it would license, and enters the distinction that keeps it from becoming a precedent. When the Amorites were put to the sword, Israel acted as the executioners of God's wrath at a moment when the measure of that nation's iniquity was full — and the longer it had been in filling, the sorer the reckoning. On his reading they died not as Israel's enemies but as sacrifices to divine justice, in the offering of which Israel served as a kingdom of priests; and because the case was extraordinary in that way, it is not to be drawn into a precedent for military executions that give no quarter. Those will have judgment without mercy, he ends, who show no mercy.

Keil and Delitzsch reach the same result from the other end without rearranging anything. That Moses sent words of peace even after being told the land was given him was done to show the king of the Amorites that the loss of his kingdom and his life was his own fault; the wish to pass through peaceably was quite seriously meant, though Moses foresaw from the divine communication that it would be refused. Henry says the same in his own idiom and guards it against misreading: Moses neither disobeyed God, who had bidden him contend with Sihon, nor dissembled with Sihon, but acted by divine direction so that the king might be left inexcusable though God hardened his heart — which he takes to illustrate God's dealing with those to whom he gives the gospel without giving grace to believe it.
26:
The place the messengers set out from can be located roughly. Gill takes Kedemoth for a city later given to the Levites, with a wilderness beside it that took its name, and reports Aben Ezra's alternative that it is the wilderness of Matthanah, which Jerome placed on the Arnon twelve miles east of Medeba; Ellicott finds the town listed among those of the plain belonging to Heshbon.

What the message meant is more consequential than where it came from. Ellicott reads it against the law of sieges that would afterwards be laid down, by which cities offered terms and cities under the ban were treated differently: by sending words of peace Moses excepted Sihon from the catalogue of doomed kings and nations, so that the fate which followed was of his own bringing. What was offered him, Ellicott adds pointedly, were the same privileges the Moabites enjoyed — the very people Sihon had conquered — and he refused the position.

The terms themselves are modest, and each commentator notes what keeps them so. Keil and Delitzsch summarise them as a promise to keep the high road and turn neither right nor left; Gill observes that they asked no provision except what they would pay for. Wesley catches the significance of a phrase easily passed over: on my feet means with a company that goes on foot, added deliberately, since an army made up largely of horsemen, as many were, would have been a far more dangerous thing to let through one's country. On the appeal to precedent Gill is careful about what is actually being claimed. Jarchi points out that neither Edom nor Moab had granted a passage through the heart of their land; what they granted was the sale of food and drink. Wesley presses the same point further and finds the credit deliberately placed: the people of Esau were kinder than their king would have had them be, and it is to the people, not the king, that the message ascribes the favour — though it is a king they are now addressing.

The refusal is where the chapter's hardest sentence falls, and the readings of it differ in nerve. Wesley takes the shortest way, glossing the hardening as God suffering the spirit to be hardened. Keil and Delitzsch call it a judgment of hardening suspended over Sihon by God, which led to his destruction. Ellicott declines to soften it and reframes it instead: God gave Sihon his strength, as he had given Pharaoh his and as he gives every man his, and Sihon was answerable for using that strength against the divine purpose. To harden a man's spirit, he argues, is no more necessarily a moral process than the hardening of steel — the very verb rendered made obstinate here is the one that says be of a good courage to Joshua. An unyielding spirit and a stout heart are good or bad by the use made of them; Sihon used his badly and Joshua used his well, and God's gift to the two was the same.

After the refusal the order to begin comes again, and Ellicott marks the pattern it belongs to: in all the conquests of Israel it is God who gives the word to open the attack. Gill places that word just after the messengers returned with their answer, and Keil and Delitzsch have Sihon come out to Jahaz once he saw the march was toward his land, gathering his people and leaving Heshbon, his capital, where he had resided.
33:
The victory itself is stated flatly, and what the commentators attend to is everything around it. Gill has the Lord deliver Sihon together with his lands. Ellicott enters a small textual note in passing: as the Hebrew is written the word should be his son rather than his sons, possibly some person of distinction. Keil and Delitzsch describe what the campaign then became — a war of extermination in which every town was laid under the ban, the whole population of men, women and children put to death, and only the flocks and herds and the material goods of the cities taken as prey. Gill marks the same division from the other side: the cattle were not destroyed but kept alive for the conquerors' own use and profit, and became their property.

Nobody here softens the destruction, and two of them go out of their way to fix its ground. Ellicott glosses the verb as devoting to destruction, making these towns what the spoil of Jericho was made, and insists the word will bear nothing less: the narrative asserts an extermination of Sihon's people by the express command of God, and such a thing could only be by divine direction. Wesley says the same more briefly and supplies the reason he takes to lie behind it — that these were part of a people devoted by the Lord of life and death to utter destruction for their abominable wickedness. Neither offers the alternative that might have been available, of treating the account as an exaggeration or the ban as a form of words.

One philological remark is the only thing the verses invite beyond that. Keil and Delitzsch read the phrase rendered city of men as meaning the town population of the men, which is what makes the clauses about the women and the little ones an addition to it rather than a repetition of it — the sentence is enumerating, not intensifying. Beyond this the narrative offers no comment at all: it lists what was destroyed and what was kept, and stops. Gill fills in only which cities are meant, Heshbon and the rest already named in the older account, and Keil and Delitzsch that the same method was followed through the whole of Sihon's kingdom. The commentators' agreement about the fact is matched by their care to say on whose authority it was done, and by their silence about how it felt to do it.
36:
The boundaries of the conquest are given by two towns and a hill country. Gill places Aroer on the border of Moab and calls it the principal city there; Keil and Delitzsch read the pair of names as marking the limits precisely — Aroer on the edge of the Arnon valley as the inclusive starting point of the land taken, and the Moabite capital in the valley as the exclusive one, with Gilead, rising near the Jabbok to the north, as the far limit. The claim that no city was too high for them they gloss as none too strong to be taken.

Ellicott brings the surveyors in and is not entirely satisfied by them. Conder identifies Aroer with a ruin on the north bank of the Wady Mojib; but Ellicott notes that the same surveyor makes the Aroer named in Numbers a different place and marks it unknown, and asks outright why. Of the second town he says only that the description suggests Rabbath-ammon and that Rabbath-ammon cannot be what is meant here.

What was not taken closes the chapter, and the restraint is the point of it. Gill runs through the exclusions — the land the Ammonites then actually held, any town on the Jabbok that formed their border, the cities of their mountain country, and in general whatever God had forbidden, in Edom or Moab or Ammon, though it is Ammon he has chiefly in view. Wesley reads the phrase about the Jabbok as meaning beyond it, that river being the Ammonite border. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same line, along the eastern side of the upper Jabbok and the towns of the Ammonite highlands, and note that whatever Sihon had earlier taken from Ammon was not covered by the prohibition, which is how Israel came to hold ground that had once been Ammonite.

Clarke draws the conclusion the whole chapter has been building toward and then follows it into later history. The commission was limited, and those only were to be cut off whose cup of iniquity was full. Moab and Ammon were spared on that principle — and requited the forbearance with evil, fighting against Israel afterwards, casting them out of their possessions and committing what he calls the most shocking cruelties. Hence, he observes, the later law that none of these people should enter the congregation of the Lord to their tenth generation. The sequence he leaves standing without comment is its own argument: the nations Israel was forbidden to touch when it had the strength to destroy them were the nations that attacked Israel when it had not.
